strengths: Clear pedagogical motivation through analytically solvable toy problem (Theorem 1, Corollary 1) that elegantly demonstrates how ill-conditioned gradients cause grokking plateaus
Remarkably simple, practical method (single SVD transformation) with no hyperparameters, no additional memory, and no scheduling requirements
Strong, consistent empirical results on standard grokking benchmarks (sparse parity, modular arithmetic) where method eliminates/drastically reduces plateau duration
Well-articulated connections to natural gradient descent and clear comparison with Grokfast, delineating advantages in memory efficiency, simplicity, and theoretical guarantees
Excellent presentation with clear structure, intuitive figures (especially Figure 4 on ill-conditioned spectra), and honest acknowledgment of limitations
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope restricted to small synthetic problems only (n≤400 for parity, p≤127 for modular arithmetic, networks with ≤512 hidden units); no experiments on naturalistic tasks despite citations to grokking on vision/language datasets

Substantial theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 applies only to linear model with engineered data distribution; connection to neural networks is purely empirical, leaving unexplained why identical mechanism works across diverse architectures/tasks
Missing critical direct experimental comparison with Grokfast, the most relevant baseline claiming grokking acceleration; Grokfast only appears in initial figures with unclear experimental setup

Computational cost analysis absent: full SVD per layer per iteration is O(min(mp², m²p)); no wall-clock measurements, no validation of 'SVD doesn't need to be precise' claim, scalability to large models undemonstrated
Grokking detection mechanism for switching from EGD to vanilla SGD is unexplained, introducing undocumented hyperparameter that somewhat undermines 'hyperparameter-free' claim
Limited ablation studies: no analysis of column normalization variant's effectiveness, approximate SVD degradation, layer-specific application, or rank-deficiency handling mentioned in Remark 1
No statistical significance testing with error bars or multiple random seeds; single-run results without variance estimates
Unaddressed disconnect between toy problem using quadratic loss and experiments using cross-entropy/hinge loss; finite-sample behavior not analyzed despite w.h.p. theoretical statements

strengths: Clear intuition through well-designed toy problem (Section 3) that motivates the method via ill-conditioned gradient spectra
Rigorous theoretical analysis (Theorem 1, Corollary 1) showing plateau length scales as O(1/ε) for the toy problem
Simple, practical algorithm with no hyperparameters, no extra memory, and easy integration into training loops
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse settings (modular arithmetic, sparse parity, MNIST, CIFAR-10, multiple architectures and optimizers)
Thoughtful ablations and variants (exact SVD, randomized SVD, column normalization) with computational efficiency analysis
Strong exposition of connections to natural gradient descent (Eq. 13) and independent convergence with Muon optimizer
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, pseudo-code, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core transformation is essentially Fisher preconditioning (a standard technique); the innovation is primarily in application rather than methodology
Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 applies only to 2D linear toy problem; convergence analysis for practical non-linear networks remains unresolved ('highly difficult')
Unclear mechanism generalization: insufficient evidence that ill-conditioning is the primary cause of grokking across all tested problems; only Figure 4 demonstrates one example

Stability concerns: Figures 14-15 show EGD with exact SVD becomes highly unstable for transformers on modular multiplication; RSVD fixes this but requires rank tuning, undermining 'hyperparameter-free' claims
Missing failure case analysis: column normalization and some RSVD variants fail on sparse parity k=4 with no principled explanation or diagnostic guidance

Mixed practical results vs Grokfast: MNIST (Table 6) shows marginal improvements (~0.9% better accuracy); transformers (Table 7) show Grokfast is faster with exact SVD; competitive performance requires RSVD rank tuning
Computational overhead not justified: wall-clock time results (Tables 2-4) show simpler column normalization often wins despite being 'simplified' EGD, and SVD adds non-trivial cost per iteration
Incomplete solution analysis: EGD converges to different parameter regions than vanilla SGD (Appendix F) with limited discussion of implications for generalization or solution preferences
Rank selection for RSVD: task-dependent optimal rank with no principled a priori selection method, introducing hyperparameter sensitivity contrary to claimed simplicity
Limited scope: strongest results on synthetic algorithmic problems; real-world grokking (vision, NLP mentioned in intro) lacks experimental support; MNIST/CIFAR-10 results show mixed performance
Practical guidance gap: no clear decision framework for practitioners on when to use EGD vs Grokfast, or which variant (SVD/RSVD/column norm) to choose

Presentation: extended length with key results in appendices; non-stationarity experiments (Appendix E) feel disconnected; toy problem (infinite samples, exact statistics) vs practical finite-sample networks gap could be clearer
